result.summary: Medea confronts Jason for planning to give her up, and together they lure her brother Apsyrtus to a temple of Artemis, where Jason kills him. The Argonauts flee, are warned by the speaking beam of the ship that Zeus is angry, and sail by the Eridanus and Rhodanus to Circe's island, where she purifies them.

scenes.title: Medea reproaches Jason
scenes.summary: Medea furiously accuses Jason of betrayal and threatens curses and burning the ship. Jason soothes her, and they agree to trap Apsyrtus.
scenes.stakes: Medea fears being handed back to her brother and father; Jason fears destruction by the Colchian host.

scenes.title: The gifts and the snare
scenes.summary: They prepare guest-gifts including Hypsipyle's robe, and Medea lures Apsyrtus with false words. The narrator laments the power of Love.
scenes.stakes: Apsyrtus is being lured into a deadly trap.

place.name: Temple of Artemis on the island

scenes.title: Murder of Apsyrtus
scenes.summary: Jason ambushes and kills Apsyrtus, and the heroes slaughter the Colchian crew. The leaderless Colchians scatter and settle in various lands.
scenes.stakes: Apsyrtus loses his life; the heroes risk blood-guilt and pursuit.

scenes.title: The Hylleans and Hyllus
scenes.summary: The Argonauts reach the Hylleans, who aid them for a tripod of Apollo. The narrator tells how Hyllus, son of Heracles, came to settle there.

scenes.title: Zeus's wrath and speaking beam
scenes.summary: Zeus is angry at the murder. Hera drives the ship back with storms, and the oak beam of Argo speaks, telling them to seek Circe's purification.
scenes.stakes: The crew face endless storms and wandering unless purified of the murder.

scenes.title: Eridanus, Rhodanus and the Celts
scenes.summary: The ship passes the Eridanus where Phaethon fell and the Heliades weep amber, then the Rhodanus. Hera turns them back from the Ocean gulf and guides them to the Stoechades and Aethalia.
scenes.stakes: They risk entering an unreturnable gulf of Ocean and dying in ignorance.

scenes.title: Circe purifies the murderers
scenes.summary: At Aeaea they find Circe shaken by dreams and followed by hybrid beasts. Seeing the silent suppliants, she performs the rite of purification.
scenes.stakes: Jason and Medea need cleansing from blood-guilt to escape the wrath of Zeus and the Furies.

Medea's reproach to Jason over broken oaths by Zeus.

analysis.text: Love and betrayal turn Medea from helper to accomplice in murder, and the blood-guilt of Apsyrtus's death shadows the voyage home.
The route through the Adriatic, Po, Rhône and western Mediterranean reflects Greek geographic knowledge and legends of the west.

legacy.text: The murder of Apsyrtus appears in later tellings of Medea, including Euripides-era and Roman versions, in varying forms.

fun_facts.text: The amber tears of the Heliades reflect an ancient link between the Po region and the amber trade.

language_notes.text: "Reekest thou nothing" is archaic for "do you care nothing"; "reek" here means to heed or regard, not to smell.
Zeus, god of suppliants, guaranteed the protection of those who begged for help; Jason's oaths to Medea were sworn in his name.
Kingfishers (halcyons) were proverbially mournful birds; Medea compares her lonely exile at sea to their cries.
"Guerdon" means reward or recompense; here bitterly ironic, since the reward for her passion would be death.
The sentence is broken off: she imagines the king, as arbiter of the covenant, awarding her back to her brother Apsyrtus.
Zeus' bride is Hera, Jason's protector and goddess of marriage and oaths, whom Medea asks not to grant his homecoming.
The Furies were avenging spirits who punished oath-breakers and wrongs against kin.
"This covenant" means the agreement to give Medea up to the king's judgment, which Jason claims is only a trap for Apsyrtus.
Dionysus gave the robe to Thoas, his son by Ariadne; Thoas became king of Lemnos, and Hypsipyle was his daughter. Hence the robe's divine descent.
The 'king of Nysa' is Dionysus; the maiden-daughter of Minos is Ariadne, abandoned by Theseus on Dia (Naxos) after helping him at Cnossus.
The Fury is an avenging spirit who punishes kin-murder and bloodshed.
The mutilation and tasting of blood was a ritual to appease the murdered man's ghost and avert vengeance from the killer.
Electra here is an island name in the northern Adriatic; the 'Minyans' in sentence 56 means the Argonauts.
Harmonia and Cadmus, the legendary founders of Thebes, were said to have ended their lives among the Encheleans in Illyria.
"Guerdon" is an archaic word for reward or payment.
Pytho is Delphi, Apollo's oracle. Aeson's son is Jason, who consulted the oracle before sailing.
"Bare" is the old past tense of "bore"; Melite bore Hyllus to Heracles.
Heracles killed his own children in a fit of madness sent by Hera, and sought cleansing for it.
The narrator addresses the Muses as "goddesses" and asks why the Argo's route is remembered so far west.
Dodona in Epirus held Zeus's oracle in an oak grove, so the beam's oak can speak prophecy.
"Minyan" refers to the Argonauts, many of whom descended from the Minyans of Iolcus and Orchomenus.
Phaethon, son of Helios, lost control of his father's sun-chariot and was struck down by Zeus's thunderbolt, falling into the Eridanus.
The Heliades, Phaethon's sisters, mourned him until they were turned into poplars; their tears became amber.
Apollo was banished by Zeus after killing the Cyclopes who forged the thunderbolt that slew his son Asclepius, born of Coronis.
Hyperboreans: a legendary people living in the far north, beyond the north wind, favoured by Apollo.
Noisome means foul-smelling or harmful.
The Hercynian rock refers to the Hercynian forest and mountains of central Europe; Hera's cry comes from there.
The sons of Zeus are Castor and Polydeuces, the Dioscuri, later honoured as protectors of sailors.
Ausonia is an old name for Italy; the Tyrrhenian shores lie along its western coast, so the Argonauts are now in the western Mediterranean.
Describes an early creation when the earth was still soft and unformed, so life emerged from slime in jumbled forms; time later sorted them into ranks.
Sitting silently at the hearth is the traditional posture of a suppliant seeking protection and purification.
Zeus protects suppliants (Zeus Hikesios) and is also angered by murder, hence 'god of wrath' who still aids slayers seeking cleansing.
Propitiation means appeasing a god; 'unexpiated' means the murder not yet atoned for. The piglet's blood was the standard purification.
The Furies are avenging spirits who pursue those guilty of kindred bloodshed; here Circe prays to hold back their wrath.

context_notes.text: Medea claims to follow Jason as child, bride and sister, stressing the ties of kinship and marriage she has given up everything for.
Apsyrtus is Medea's brother, prince of Colchis, pursuing the Argonauts to recover her and the fleece.
Apsyrtus is Medea's brother, leading the Colchian pursuit. The 'guest-gifts' are bait to draw him to a meeting.
The agreement left Medea on Artemis's island as a pledge while both sides landed separately.
Hera protects the Argonauts throughout the poem, favouring Jason.
Jason and Medea had treacherously killed Medea's brother Apsyrtus; Zeus is angered by the bloodshed, which required ritual purification.
Circe, Medea's aunt, was a sorceress on the western Italian coast, known for purifying killers.
Hera favors Jason and the Argonauts, so she acts to steer them toward the cleansing Zeus requires.
The Rhodanus is the Rhone. Ancient writers imagined a river system linking it with the Eridanus, which was often placed in the Po or the far north.
The Ligyans (Ligurians) lived along the coast of what is now southern France and northwest Italy.
Aethalia is the island of Elba; the pebbles and the Argoan harbour were explained as traces of the Argonauts' visit.
Circe is the sister of Aeetes and a sorceress, aunt of Medea. Her island Aeaea is where Jason and Medea seek cleansing for killing Apsyrtus.
Aeetes' son is Apsyrtus, Medea's brother, whom Jason killed in an ambush; this is the murder needing purification.
Naiads are nymphs of springs and waters, fitting attendants for a rite of washing away guilt.

literary_notes.text: Her list of lost home, glories and parents, ending in lonely exile, stirs sympathy and sharpens the charge against Jason.
The fleece vanishing like a dream compares his prize to something insubstantial, wishing his triumph to prove empty.
Hostile men are likened to a surrounding fire, conveying danger and also echoing Medea's own burning anger.
Weaving a "web of guile" pictures deceit as craftwork, foreshadowing the treacherous murder of Apsyrtus.
Her cold "I care not" shows Medea's shift from wounded lover to ruthless accomplice, darkening her portrait.
The narrator breaks off to address Love directly, blaming the god for Medea's crime.
Apsyrtus testing his sister is compared to a child trying a torrent, hinting at his naive, fatal risk.
Medea's covering her eyes shows her lingering shame even as she takes part in the betrayal.
Comparing the killing to a butcher felling a bull makes the murder a brutal, dishonourable slaughter.
Kites among wood-pigeons and lions among sheep stress the helplessness of the Colchians.
The narrator turns to the Muses for help, a traditional epic invocation that marks a shift to a new, difficult topic.
The ship's beam speaks with a human voice, making the Argo an active, prophetic character.
The crew's terror anticipates the long, hard wanderings they must endure before Circe's purification.
The weeping poplar-maidens and their amber tears turn grief into a lasting natural wonder and evoke pity.
Tears drifting on the water like drops of oil makes the sisters' grief visible and strange.
Hera's cry shakes the heavens themselves, showing divine power directing the heroes' course.
The mist that Hera pours around the ship stands for divine protection that hides the heroes from danger.
Blood-streaming walls and flame consuming her herbs signal omens of violence and the failing of her magic, foreshadowing the arrival of murderers.
The hybrid beasts following Circe are compared to sheep trailing a shepherd, showing her mastery over them while making them look eerie yet docile.
Circe is recognized as Aeetes' sister by her face alone, marking family likeness and her uncanny, kin-linked authority.
The silent, lowered-eyed pair reveal their guilt without a word; Circe, a kinswoman, reads it immediately.
